projects.title: Budgetmo
projects.description: Khaled Eltokhy's rendering of New York City's $125.8 billion budget as a Venmo-style mobile feed -- a scrollable transaction stream inside a simulated phone frame, with category filters and a search bar. The feed carries real line items from the adopted budget: Council discretionary funding (Schedule C member items), the citywide expense budget and what actually got paid, FY2015 through FY2027. Eltokhy spent two and a half years as a research analyst in the International Monetary Fund's Fiscal Affairs Department and teaches economics at Hunter College and Baruch College. Surfaced in BetaNYC's July 23 civic-tech roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Borrows the interface grammar of a consumer payment app to make municipal spending legible to people who would never open a budget PDF -- a design argument that the barrier to fiscal transparency is format, not access.

projects.title: City Ledger
projects.description: Dashboard billed as the New York City government ledger and grant matcher, showing how the city distributed funding across the five boroughs over nearly two decades, with an AI grant-matching feature layered on top. Built on BetaNYC's own New York City budget dataset -- the twenty-year Schedule C compilation released earlier this month. Featured in BetaNYC's July 23 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Turns the raw discretionary-award archive into a geographic question: which parts of the city got the money. The grant matcher points the same data at nonprofits looking for funding, so the ledger works as both accountability record and service.

projects.title: Gothamist: Every Upper East Side cooling tower, mapped
projects.description: Gothamist map of all 179 cooling towers in the Carnegie Hill and Yorkville ZIP codes (10028, 10075, 10128) at the center of a Legionnaires' disease cluster of at least 14 cases, built from city inspection and Legionella test records. The accompanying analysis of Department of Health and Mental Hygiene data found the city had inspected 1,306 of roughly 6,000 cooling towers citywide since the start of 2026, that 48 percent of towers inside the outbreak ZIP codes had gone more than a year without a city inspection, and that about 26 percent had no record of owner testing in 2026.
projects.why_interesting: Regulatory-compliance data, mapped at the building level during a live outbreak -- the rare case where an open dataset about inspection backlogs becomes immediately actionable for the people living inside the affected blocks.

projects.title: NYC Building Footprints
projects.description: The Office of Technology and Innovation's citywide building footprint layer, spotlighted in BetaNYC's July 23 roundup as the dataset of the week. It tracked 1,082,974 buildings as of July 13, 2026, with features updated daily by staff and released publicly on NYC Open Data and NYCMaps. Roughly 93 percent of measurements come from photogrammetry -- 3D geometry derived from annual oblique aerial imagery plus ground-level panoramic photography -- and 95 percent of footprints are accurate to within two feet. Each record carries a status: constructed, demolition, alteration, geometry, correction, marked for construction, marked for demolition or initialization.
projects.why_interesting: The status field is the underused part: it makes the footprint layer a near-real-time record of what is going up and coming down, not just a static basemap. Nearly every geospatial project in the city rests on this layer whether or not its builders realize it.

projects.title: NYC Internet Access Survey
projects.description: Open city survey collecting resident responses on home and mobile internet access, cost and reliability, intended to shape digital-equity policy and investment priorities. Promoted in BetaNYC's July 23 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: The city's broadband picture has leaned on federal Census and Federal Communications Commission estimates that miss affordability and reliability entirely. A first-party survey is how the gap between having a connection and being able to use it gets measured.

projects.title: NYC Agencies and Governance Organizations
projects.description: NYC Open Data reference dataset listing city agencies, offices and other organizations with New York City governance functions -- advisory and regulatory bodies, public benefit and development corporations, elected offices, mayoral agencies and offices, nonprofit organizations and state agencies operating in the city. Last updated July 16, 2026.
projects.why_interesting: There has never been a single authoritative machine-readable list of what counts as a New York City government entity, which is why spending and staffing analyses keep disagreeing on the denominator. This is the crosswalk that fixes that.

projects.title: Axiom Foundation
projects.description: Ariel Kennan's new effort to publish open, machine-readable encodings of tax and benefit law -- cited, time-aware and executable -- launching publicly July 28, 2026 with a virtual briefing. It releases two paired layers: version-controlled source documents (statutes, regulations, guidance from authoritative sources) and encodings in which every value cites a statute and every clause carries effective dates. An AI pipeline reads a statute, encodes it subsection by subsection, validates the output against independent oracles including PolicyEngine and TAXSIM and logs discrepancies before a human signs off. Kennan spent a decade building service design inside government; BetaNYC named her its Public Interest Technologist of the Month on July 23.
projects.why_interesting: Every benefit calculator and tax program already translates law into code, almost always privately and unverifiably. Publishing that translation layer in the open, with citations attached, is a structural fix rather than another calculator -- and the oracle-validation step is a serious answer to the obvious objection about trusting AI with statute.

projects.title: Transparent.city
projects.description: Platform that converts municipal open data into plain-language, source-linked findings with charts. The Chicago instance draws on 2,003 public datasets and tracks crime (drug crimes down 21 percent year to date, violent crimes down 9 percent, homicides up 2 percent), business registrations, building and residential construction permits, traffic crashes and 311 complaints -- reporting, for instance, 28,830 pothole complaints through July 22, 2026, up 40.9 percent from 20,458 in the same 2025 period, and aircraft noise at 21.4 percent of all 311 requests. The site invites other cities to be added.
projects.why_interesting: Most city dashboards stop at the chart and leave interpretation to the reader. This one writes the sentence -- with the source link attached -- which is the harder and more useful half, and the piece that actually travels into local reporting.

projects.title: Transit Costs Project: 2026 data update
projects.description: New York University Marron Institute's refreshed global rail-construction cost database, now covering 755 lines broken into 1,020 phases across 202 cities in 60 countries, totaling 20,809 kilometers (12,930 miles). Costs are purchasing-power-parity and inflation adjusted to 2025 dollars; the weighted average is $252.28 million per kilometer, or $406.01 million per mile. The official version now lives in New York University's Ultraviolet Repository with a DOI for citation. The project notes the data covers only a portion of rail projects in each city or country.
projects.why_interesting: The reference dataset behind nearly every argument about why American transit costs what it does, and the DOI move makes it properly citable. The per-kilometer weighted average is the number to hold up against any New York City megaproject figure.

projects.title: US Digital Response SNAP Payment Accuracy Playbook
projects.description: Living resource for state agencies facing the payment-error-rate cost-sharing provisions in H.R.1 of the 119th Congress, updated periodically with state-level SNAP payment accuracy data and error rates. Built on hands-on research conducted September 2025 through February 2026 with Arizona's Department of Economic Security, North Carolina's Department of Health and Human Services and Maryland's Family Investment Administration, and expanded to eight states as of March 2026. Its findings point at eligibility-system usability, weak internal feedback loops and client communications as the root causes, and argue that catching errors before benefits go out is the highest-impact intervention. States have until September 2026 to show progress. Surfaced again in BetaNYC's July 23 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: A rare piece of benefits research that names the software as the problem -- the argument that policy guidance belongs inside the caseworker's eligibility screen rather than in a memo is a design claim with a federal funding penalty attached to it.

projects.title: BetaNYC: NYC mayoral executive orders archive
projects.description: Open, machine-readable archive of New York City mayoral executive orders, created July 11, 2026 and pushed to daily since. The repository frames itself as supplying the compilation that New York City Administrative Code section 3-113.1 requires the city to publish.
projects.why_interesting: Executive orders are how a mayor governs between legislation and budget, and they have never existed as a structured, queryable set. Building it as an explicit stand-in for a legally mandated compilation the city has not produced makes the repo an accountability artifact as much as a dataset.

projects.title: BetaNYC: Grounding AI with New York open data
projects.description: Repository created July 7, 2026 collecting Socrata Model Context Protocol configurations, a directory of New York City and New York State open data portals and guides for pointing AI agents at authentic city and state data rather than letting them improvise. Sits alongside BetaNYC's connector work for the Council, 311, the City Record, the Charter and Administrative Code and New York State legislation.
projects.why_interesting: The failure mode for AI on civic questions is confident invention. This is the practical countermeasure -- configuration and portal plumbing that keeps an agent answering from the actual dataset, which is exactly the layer that determines whether the next wave of civic AI tools is trustworthy.
